claims.text: The baseline W-Ta-Cr-V refractory high-entropy alloy has high-temperature strength.

The baseline W-Ta-Cr-V alloy has an enhanced irradiation response compared with previously developed W-based alloys, including no noticeable dislocation loops, smaller He bubbles, and no grain-boundary radiation-induced segregation under the reported irradiation conditions.
Adding a controlled amount of Hf to W-Ta-Cr-V will improve its mechanical performance under high-temperature and irradiation conditions.
Hf addition increases lattice distortion in W-Ta-Cr-V.
The Hf-induced lattice distortion enhances solid-solution strengthening.
Hf modifies defect mobility and recombination in irradiated W-Ta-Cr-V.
Hf addition can reduce the size of irradiation-induced defect clusters such as He bubbles.
Hf has a high melting point and a large atomic size.
Hf promotes solid-solution hardening and modifies defect-formation kinetics in W-Ta-Cr-V.
Hf slows the mobility of radiation-induced defects, including dislocation loops, and suppresses bubble growth.
Relative to W-Ta-Cr-V, the Hf-modified alloy will have higher yield strength.
Relative to W-Ta-Cr-V, the Hf-modified alloy will have improved room-temperature and high-temperature ductility.
The Hf-modified alloy will retain thermal stability while improving strength and ductility.
The beneficial effects occur only within a moderate Hf-content range.
Excessive Hf may cause unwanted phase formation or segregation.
The optimum Hf concentration and its long-term behavior under cyclic thermal and irradiation exposure have not been quantified.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement, exemplified by roughly a 10% yield-strength increase or a measurable reduction in defect size or density, would falsify the hypothesis.
